# Controls
Controls is a specification that defines the game options and reproduction tools in Neon Pairs.

Status: spec version 2.2.

You can start another deal, repeat the current one or load saved progress. Each control keeps the same label, so you can find the same action after a game changes.

## Deal controls

The main controls are:

- C01 - Label the native size select "Grid size". Give it options `4x4`, `6x6`, `8x8`, `10x10`, `12x12`, `14x14` and `16x16`, with numeric side length `N` as each value. After a successful board-code or snapshot load, select the loaded board's size.
- C02 - Label the fresh-deal button "New Game". It creates a fresh seed and keeps the current size.
- C03 - Label the repeat-deal button "Restart". It starts the same board code again.

Changing size, starting and restarting follow the session rules in Rules.

## Reproduction tools

- C04 - Put reproduction controls inside a native `details` element that starts collapsed. Give its summary the exact text "Reproduce a game".

The controls use the board-code and snapshot formats defined in Reproducibility. A board code starts a deal. A snapshot loads progress on a deal.

## Load a board

- C05 - Label the text input "Board code" and limit it to 32 characters. Show the current board code after a new deal, Restart or a successful load. Keep an edited draft when a card action changes the game.

- C06 - Label its button "Load board". Validate the entered code before replacing the current game with that deal's starting state.

For example, loading `np1-4-1` starts its hidden four-column board. Entering that code alone keeps the current game until you select Load board.

## Snapshot tools

- C07 - Label the textarea "Snapshot JSON" and limit it to 65536 characters. The parser also applies the UTF-8 byte limit in the snapshot format.

- C08 - Label the export button "Export snapshot". Fill the textarea with readable version 1 snapshot JSON that you can select and copy manually. Export leaves the game state and clock unchanged. It requires no Clipboard API.

Export `elapsedMs` and a pending mismatch's `remainingMs` as whole milliseconds. A pending mismatch always exports at least 1ms.

- C09 - Label the import button "Load snapshot". Validate the complete draft before replacing the current game. Load unfinished progress paused and show "Loaded snapshot. Select Resume to continue." Load completed progress as completed without pausing and show "Loaded completed snapshot."

- C10 - Show a "Resume" button only while an imported unfinished game is paused. Selecting it clears that pause. Unfinished play continues from the loaded state. While paused, block every card activation and allow board focus movement. On Resume, move focus to the board's remembered tab stop before removing the Resume button. A loaded completed game stays completed and shows no Resume button.

- C11 - On invalid input, keep the current game and the entered draft for correction. Show the exact status for that control:

| Control | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Load board | Invalid board code. |
| Load snapshot | Invalid snapshot. |

- C12 - A loaded completed snapshot keeps the win banner static and plays no celebration. Import doesn't write a best score. Resuming an unfinished snapshot and later winning records a local best under R10.

For example, loading a completed game with fewer moves than the saved best shows that game without replacing the saved record.

## Focus

- C13 - Keep focus on the button used for starting, restarting, loading or exporting. These actions don't move focus to the board. Resume follows C10 because its button disappears. The board's remembered tab stop follows the focus rules in Input.

## Replay

- C14 - Keep replay in the developer CLI and game core. V1 has no replay controls in the game UI.

Run `npm run --silent replay -- PATH` to read a replay file. On valid input, print only the final snapshot JSON to stdout and exit 0. On invalid input, print nothing to stdout, write a message to stderr and exit nonzero.

The complete game pack starts in Neon Pairs.
# Input
Input is a set of controls that lets you play Neon Pairs with a pointer, touch or keyboard.

Status: spec version 2.2.

You can reveal a card with a tap, then move to its partner with the arrow keys. Every activation uses the same game action, so changing input methods keeps the same turn.

## Activation

The card controls follow these rules:

- I01 - Render each card as a native button. A primary click, a completed tap, Enter and Space activate the card through the same action.
- I03 - Keep the browser's normal context menu on right-click or long-press. Opening that menu doesn't activate a card.
- I04 - Hover and pointer cancellation leave the game state unchanged.

The game decides whether an activation changes a card. See Rules for matches, repeated selections, blocked turns and turn timing.

## Keyboard movement

- I05 - Give the board one remembered tab stop. When Tab enters the board, focus that card. Use the first card before any board focus has been remembered.

- I06 - Move focus with these keys. Movement changes focus without activating a card:

| Key | Focus destination |
| --- | --- |
| ArrowLeft | Previous card in the same row |
| ArrowRight | Next card in the same row |
| ArrowUp | Card in the previous row and same column |
| ArrowDown | Card in the next row and same column |

The board handles only these four arrow keys without modifiers, plus Enter and Space. It leaves every other key and modifier combination to the browser and doesn't use them to move focus or activate a card.

- I07 - Stop arrow movement at a board edge. Moving left from the first column keeps focus on the same card.

- I08 - Let native Tab and Shift+Tab leave the board. Moving through the board uses the movement keys instead of adding every card to the page's tab order.

## Focus

The board keeps focus separate from play:

- I09 - Keep matched cards focusable and mark them `aria-disabled="true"`. Their game action follows the matched-card rule in the gameplay document.
- I10 - While a mismatching pair waits to turn back, allow focus movement and block card activation.
- I11 - On initial load, keep the browser's current focus. Loading the game doesn't move focus to the board.
- I12 - After a new deal, Restart or a successful load, reset the board's remembered tab stop to its first card.
- I13 - When a card receives focus, scroll it into view with nearest alignment in the board's scroll area. Give each card a scroll margin of at least 6px, so its complete focus outline stays in view, including mid-board cards.

The session buttons keep their focus as defined in Controls.

## Card names

The button names describe the information available to the player:

- I14 - Name a hidden card by its one-based row, column and closed state. Keep its face SVG and face identifier out of the DOM while it is hidden, including attributes and accessible text.
- I15 - Name a revealed or matched card by its position, face name and state. Use the face names defined in Visuals.

For example, the first hidden button is named "Row 1, column 1, closed". Once revealed, its name includes the face, so a player can remember it without seeing the drawing.

## Announcements

- I16 - Use one polite, atomic live region for turn results and completion. Announce each turn result exactly once. A winning turn has one announcement containing both the match and the win. Consecutive identical results each get their own announcement. Focus movement, clock renders and closing a mismatch don't repeat a result.

Use these turn announcements, where `M` is the matched pair count, `N` is moves and `time` uses R07's display format:

| Event | Announcement |
| --- | --- |
| First match | Pair found. 1 pair matched. |
| Later match | Pair found. M pairs matched. |
| Miss | No match. Cards close after a short pause. |
| Final match | Pair found. All pairs found in N moves and time. |

Send the load statuses in Controls through this same live region once per load event. Keep the visible status beside the reproduction controls.

For example, moving across three cards leaves the current announcement unchanged. Resolving the next pair announces that turn's result.

## Screen reader

- I17 - Support a complete 4x4 keyboard game with a screen reader. Find Grid size and New Game by name, enter the board, expose closed positions and revealed faces by name and state, announce one result per turn and make the win, final moves and time available. Leave the board with Tab and start another game. Deliver automated accessibility-tree evidence for this journey. Record the browser and tool versions in the project README and say whether a screen reader was used. If one was used, record its name and version. The user confirms spoken output during acceptance. Spoken confirmation isn't the developer's deliverable.

The complete game pack starts in Neon Pairs.
# Time policy

This page describes how Neon Pairs accounts for active play time and keeps browser timing separate from logical game transitions.

There are three related values to distinguish: a browser observation, the delta between observations and the elapsed milliseconds stored in a game. The browser adapter observes; the clock arithmetic determines a delta; the rules apply that delta. The displayed statistic is derived from stored elapsed time rather than from a second independent stopwatch.

## Where observations enter

`use-session-clock.ts` owns browser observation and scheduling. Its neighbor `browser-clock.ts` accepts observations as arguments and computes a numerical step. Game code reads time only through the session clock. Only files in src/game/session/ may call performance.now, and no game code may use Date. Rule functions therefore receive elapsed amounts directly and can be exercised without a wall clock.

This boundary does not mean every file in the session directory performs an observation. `session.ts` transforms data and delegates logical advancement to `advanceGame`. `browser-clock.ts` creates an observation record from a supplied number. Their placement keeps time-related behavior together while the browser hook contains the actual calls.

The tests have their own environment control. Browser fixtures can install a Playwright clock and test scripts can set the observation that the application sees. Those are verification mechanisms outside the game source, not additional application clocks.

## Conditions for active time

The hook's `running()` predicate reads the latest session ref. It returns true only when the document is considered visible, the session is not paused, the game has started and the game is not won. The rules independently refuse to advance a game that has not started or has already been won.

A first accepted card activation sets `started` to true. The synchronization before that activation treats the preceding wait as inactive. The next active observation can therefore measure from the activation boundary rather than from page load. Repeated activation of the same revealed card is ignored by the rules but synchronization still accounts for time that passed before the attempted action.

An unfinished imported snapshot is paused by `replaceGame`. Its saved elapsed time and mismatch remainder remain game data, while the session prevents further active advancement until Resume. Resume resets the observation baseline and clears pause-related notices. It does not restart the imported game or give a pending mismatch a new full interval.

Completed games stop logical advancement. A completed imported game is already won, so it does not acquire an active timer. Completion through a final match is synchronized before that match, which makes the final stored elapsed time reflect play up to the finishing activation.

## Delta arithmetic

`ActiveClock` stores `observedAt`. `createClock(now)` creates that record. `elapsedStep(clock, now, active)` computes `delta = now - clock.observedAt`; it returns the delta only when active, finite and positive. Otherwise it returns zero. In both cases it returns a new clock whose baseline is `now`.

Advancing the baseline during an inactive observation is essential. Suppose the last active observation was 100ms, the page becomes hidden at 150ms and becomes visible at 5150ms. The hidden-to-visible event synchronizes while the stored visibility flag is still false. That step contributes zero and moves the baseline to 5150ms, so the following active observation excludes the hidden interval.

The arithmetic keeps fractional milliseconds. There is no per-observation integer rounding or tick counter. Several submillisecond positive deltas can add up just as one longer delta would. The tests compare totals with a floating-point tolerance where necessary.

A backward observation or a nonfinite delta produces no advancement. This is defensive handling of supplied values, not a claim that such a sequence is a normal browser clock behavior. The clock still records the supplied observation, so later arithmetic is based on that new baseline. Clock design discusses this small function and the hook separately.

## Scheduling is an opportunity to observe

`CLOCK_INTERVAL_MS` is 40. The hook uses a timeout that reschedules itself. For a mismatch it asks for the smaller of 40 and `remainingMs`; otherwise it uses 40. A scheduled delay is not added directly to the game. When the callback runs, the hook obtains a new observation and computes the actual delta.

This difference handles delayed callbacks. If the browser runs a 40ms timeout after 80ms, the measured active interval is 80ms. The rules are not told that exactly one nominal tick occurred. Conversely, receiving more callbacks does not make time pass faster, because each callback advances from the previous observation.

When the running predicate is false, scheduling stops. The visibility listener remains available to re-evaluate the state on return. Changes to generation, start state, pause state and victory also affect the hook's effect lifecycle. React rerenders alone do not supply elapsed milliseconds.

## Synchronize at action boundaries

The controller calls `clock.synchronize()` before `activateSession`. That ordering can close an overdue mismatch before the new activation is evaluated. A busy browser can delay the scheduled callback, but it does not make a logically expired interval block the next click indefinitely.

The controller also synchronizes before exporting a snapshot. Rendered state can trail the current clock by part of a scheduled interval. Serializing that rendered state directly would make exports depend on when the last render occurred. The controller instead encodes `current.current.game` after synchronization.

Fresh deals, restart, valid board loads and valid snapshot loads reset the observation baseline before replacing the game. Resume resets it before unpausing. Invalid load attempts publish a notice but do not replace the game or reset its baseline. The eventual valid synchronization still accounts for the active interval during that interaction.

## Mismatch time and elapsed time

`advanceGame` ignores a nonfinite, zero or negative amount. For a started unfinished game it adds a positive amount to `elapsedMs`, capped at `ELAPSED_MAX_MS = 359_999_999`. If the selection is a mismatch, it also subtracts the amount from `remainingMs`.

A positive remainder keeps the mismatch with its new remainder. A zero or negative remainder closes the selection. The function does not carry a queue of delayed closing events, and it does not truncate elapsed advancement to the mismatch remainder. A 900ms advance against an 800ms mismatch closes it and adds 900ms of active elapsed time.

The mismatch remainder and elapsed total serve different purposes. The total can reach its cap while a new mismatch still has time to resolve. `advanceGame` continues processing the selection even after the total is capped. Similarly, the move cap does not stop matching, time or victory. These limits protect stored/displayed numbers rather than ending play.

The 800ms mismatch interval is defined beside turn resolution as `MISMATCH_MS`. Browser scheduling reads the current remainder; snapshot validation imports the same bound. Mismatch interval covers the player-visible rule, while this page explains how the interval survives browser lifecycle events.

## Serialization has a rounding boundary

Active play retains fractions. `encodeSnapshot` floors `elapsedMs` and rounds a mismatch's `remainingMs` upward. A positive remainder smaller than one millisecond therefore exports as 1, preserving a valid pending interval. Rounding the remainder downward could produce a mismatch object with a zero value that the decoder rejects.

The decoder accepts only nonnegative safe integer elapsed values within the cap and a mismatch remainder from 1 through 800. This means the serialized representation is intentionally coarser than the in-memory state. The rounding happens at export, not after every callback.

The display uses `formatElapsed`, which floors to whole seconds and derives minutes and a two-digit seconds component. That formatter is presentation; it does not determine when cards close or when a game finishes. Elapsed time rules covers the visible statistic and limit.

## Deal generations and stale work

Every `replaceGame` call increments `generation`. A scheduled callback captures the generation from its effect. The hook checks that captured generation before observation, and `tickSession` checks it again before applying a delta. An earlier deal's callback cannot spend time in the replacement deal through the normal path.

The effect also has an `active` flag. Cleanup marks it false, clears the timeout and removes the visibility listener. The flag handles callbacks associated with a retired effect; the generation handles replacement ownership. These are related protections with different scopes.

Restarting the same board still changes the generation. Reusing the same code does not mean reusing the old progress or pending browser work. `Game.tsx` also keys `Board` by generation, which resets local board focus state on replacement. This shares a lifecycle marker without putting focus inside the time model.

## Test evidence

Arithmetic, session transitions and browser integration have separate checks. The clock suite covers fractions, inactivity and observation frequency; the session suite covers pause and generations; browser journeys cover between-tick export, overdue clicks, hidden intervals and teardown. Clock design follows those cases in detail, and Test policy explains the runners.

# Shared-device competition

This page explains the purpose, scope and implementation context of shared-device competition in Neon Pairs.

Competition gives a group gathered around one device a reason to return to the board together. It is intended for the small social setting: a family laptop, a tablet passed around a table, or a few people taking a break at the same desk. The interesting product question is how individual memory play becomes a shared occasion without losing the clarity of the existing game.

## Where the product stands

The game implements solo play. There is no competition entry form, bracket view, participant model or tournament controller in `src/game/Game.tsx`. That component composes the ordinary controls, status, board and reproduction panel around `useGame()`. Competition is a product extension that has not yet shipped.

This distinction matters during review. A prototype can show a convincing bracket around the existing board while still delegating all game actions to the ordinary session. That demonstrates a possible composition, but it says little about whether participant progress, handoffs and completion belong to the same coherent experience. The detailed pages identify the relevant behavior and the places where the current source offers support or creates a complication.

The existing specification is version 2.2. It describes a local browser memory game, its reproducibility tools and its browser session. It does not describe a competition flow. The additional decisions for this scope live in the linked competition pages; this overview introduces their purpose without reproducing them.

## Why share a device

A shared screen makes the activity visible. People can talk about the artwork, remember a near miss and recognize the effort behind another person's finish. There is no remote opponent waiting behind a network connection, and no account setup between the group and the game. The game already has a compact delivery model: the built game can be opened from one HTML file.

Sharing hardware also changes what people expect. On a personal device, a result feels like part of that person's practice. On a shared tablet, the person holding it may have changed several times since the page opened. A familiar status area can therefore carry a different social meaning even when its numbers are technically correct. The distinction between a person's current attempt, the group's progress and the device's ordinary records is especially easy to blur.

Competition is useful when it gives those existing actions a context people can follow. It is less useful when the group spends more attention administering the session than remembering cards. This is why the research discussion concentrates on interruptions, orientation and the physical act of passing the device, rather than treating the bracket drawing as the whole feature.

## Three things people are following

An individual concentrating on a board is following card positions and remembered faces. Someone waiting nearby is following the social event: who is occupied, whether a finish is close and when attention will return to the group. The person explaining the game is following the application itself, often watching for a control that might replace the current position.

These perspectives overlap, but they are not interchangeable. A board full of exposed faces is meaningful to the current player. It gives a waiting person relatively little information about where the group is in its event. A compact event view can answer that social question, while the ordinary board remains the place where the player thinks.

The competition documents separate these subjects so that readers can find the relevant decision without extracting it from a long screen-by-screen walkthrough. Pairing covers the relationship between entrants and the bracket. Rounds covers event stages. Boards and deals distinguish the dimensions of a board from its actual arrangement. Ties and scores address results from different angles.

## A local social activity, with local evidence

The current project has no backend or account service. Its board codes and exported progress are useful for reproducing a situation, not for establishing the identity of a person who played it. That is a comfortable fit for a group that is physically present and can see what happened. It is a much weaker basis for claims about distant strangers.

The same limitation applies to development evidence. A replay can help an engineer understand a sequence of card actions. A screenshot can help someone understand what the group saw. Neither explains why a participant handed the tablet back early, or whether someone had been watching another person's screen. Those are observations about the setting, and they belong in the research account rather than in an assertion about the game engine.

Reproducibility explains the existing technical tools. Competition research describes local sessions and the limits of drawing conclusions from them. The two accounts answer different questions and are useful together.

## How the current code helps

The core already separates game data from presentation. `src/game/game.ts` contains card transitions and logical elapsed time. `src/game/deck.ts` contains board parsing and deterministic generation. Those files have no participant knowledge. That makes them a useful basis for discussing competition without embedding group administration into card rendering.

The browser session is a separate layer under `src/game/session`. It owns the bridge between that core and React, browser visibility, clock observations and preferences. This is the most consequential boundary for an extension: reusing a visual component is easy to notice, while inheriting a session side effect can remain hidden until much later.

The board itself lives under `src/game/board`. Its card buttons and navigation code operate on positions. The status view receives a game and a best value; it does not discover an event or a participant. Architecture, session module and React boundaries give the broader engineering context.

import { expect } from './browser-test.ts';
import { fileURLToPath } from 'node:url';
import { isJsonObject } from '../src/game/saved-format.ts';
import { EXAMPLE_CODE, EXAMPLE_PAIRS } from '../src/game/game.fixture.ts';
import { ReproductionControl } from '../src/game/controls/control-labels.ts';
import { StatusLabel } from '../src/game/status/status-labels.ts';
import type { Page } from '@playwright/test';

export const GAME_URL = new URL('../dist/index.html', import.meta.url).href;
export const ART_URL = new URL('../.art/index.html', import.meta.url).href;
export const SESSION_URL = new URL('../.session/index.html', import.meta.url).href;
export const PHONE = { width: 360, height: 800 };
const CLOCK_START = new Date('2026-01-01T00:00:00Z');
const CLOCK_PAUSE = new Date(CLOCK_START.getTime() + 60_000);

export async function loadFixedBoard(page: Page, url = GAME_URL): Promise<void> {
  await page.goto(url);
  await page.locator('summary').click();
  await page.getByLabel(ReproductionControl.board, { exact: true }).fill(EXAMPLE_CODE);
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: ReproductionControl.loadBoard, exact: true }).click();
  await page.locator('summary').click();
  await expect(page.locator('.card')).toHaveCount(16);
}

export async function loadTimedBoard(page: Page, url = GAME_URL): Promise<void> {
  await page.clock.install({ time: CLOCK_START });
  await loadFixedBoard(page, url);
  await page.clock.pauseAt(CLOCK_PAUSE);
}

export async function exportedSnapshot(page: Page): Promise<Record<string, unknown>> {
  await page.locator('summary').click();
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: ReproductionControl.exportSnapshot, exact: true }).click();
  const value: unknown = JSON.parse(
    await page.getByLabel(ReproductionControl.snapshot, { exact: true }).inputValue(),
  );
  await page.locator('summary').click();
  if (!isJsonObject(value)) throw new Error('Expected an exported snapshot object.');
  return value;
}

export async function moves(page: Page): Promise<number> {
  return Number(
    await page
      .locator('.stats > div')
      .filter({ has: page.getByText(StatusLabel.moves, { exact: true }) })
      .locator('dd')
      .textContent(),
  );
}

export async function finishBoard(page: Page): Promise<void> {
  for (const pair of EXAMPLE_PAIRS)
    for (const index of pair) await page.locator('.card').nth(index).click();
  await expect(page.locator('.card.matched')).toHaveCount(EXAMPLE_PAIRS.length * 2);
}

## duplicate-names-policy
# Duplicate names policy

This page explains the group-level name comparison policy and the distinctions a reviewer needs when checking it.

The current source has no name list or group editor. A board code identifies a deal, a card label identifies a position and face state, and a local best is indexed by board size. None of those is a collection of person-entered names. The policy below belongs to a feature that introduces such a collection.

## Comparison boundary

The group being edited supplies the comparison scope; the draft alone cannot establish whether it repeats an existing entry. The candidate's accepted representation comes from Text entry policy. Names in one group compare without regard to case, after normalization. A repeat blocks the action and shows "Each name must be different." This lets the same visible spelling with different capitalization be recognized as a repeat without requiring that all displayed names be rewritten in one case.

The scope is one group. Neon Pairs has no global name registry across devices, browser origins or unrelated groups. A local comparison can answer whether an entry repeats within the group being acted on without implying that the person owns a unique account name.

The check concerns names, rather than board positions or face identities. Two cards intentionally share a face, and a replay can intentionally activate the same position more than once. Those repetitions follow their own game rules. A generic “remove duplicates everywhere” helper would not express this policy's subject or scope.

## Display value and comparison value

## announcements-policy
# Announcements policy

This page describes how event feedback is published, repeated and kept separate from routine game rendering.

The game has many visible updates, but only some represent a new result. A clock tick is a changing value; resolving a turn is an event. Treating those as the same kind of update would make a memory game noisy and would bury the information a player needs after selecting two cards.

## Publication point

`Game.tsx` places the game result between the board instructions and the Board itself. Its paragraph has `role="status"`, `aria-live="polite"` and `aria-atomic="true"`, with the current feedback inside a span. The page has exactly one live region, the status paragraph in Game.tsx. New status text, such as whose turn it is, goes through that region. The current game publishes pair results and load outcomes there; it has no turn-owner feature.

The paragraph remains mounted while its content changes. It is inside `.game-result`, which has a minimum height of `56px`, flex alignment and margins. The wrapper reserves a readable area near the board without making the scrollable card content itself the announcement source.

Polite publication allows the browser and assistive technology to schedule the result around other speech. Atomic content indicates that the paragraph's result is treated as a complete update rather than an isolated changed number. These attributes express the intended exposure; the actual spoken experience still needs user acceptance with a screen reader.

## Session data behind the paragraph

## focus-policy
# Focus policy

This page records focus behavior in the current game and the policy for a feature that changes the main screen.

Focus tells a keyboard user where input will go next. It is related to game selection but is not stored as part of a turn or snapshot. The current interface deliberately keeps deal-action focus, remembered board focus and card reveal state as distinct things.

## Existing page and future screens

`Game.tsx` currently renders one main area with an h1, deal controls, statistics, instructions, turn output, the Board and reproduction controls. It has no alternate-screen branch or screen-level h2 focus target. Replacing a deal remounts the board within that page; it does not replace the page with a different screen.

A feature that introduces a screen replacement has a different orientation problem from resetting a deck. When a feature replaces what the main area shows, focus moves to that screen's h2, which has tabindex="-1". This gives the new screen a programmatic landing place without adding that heading to ordinary Tab traversal. The current deal and load callbacks can still be understood on their own terms; they are not evidence that such a screen transition already exists.

The policy applies to the feature-level replacement described here. Expanding native details, updating statistics, closing a mismatch or displaying the completed-game paragraph does not currently create a new screen. Those operations retain the page structure and follow the existing behavior below. Dialog policy covers a separate interaction with its own opening focus.

## Initial load is quiet

## tables-policy
# Tables policy

This page records the markup policy for ordered result data and explains why the current game statistics use a different structure.

There is no result table in the current UI. `GameStatus.tsx` displays four properties of a single game in a definition list. Reproduction controls use forms, and the board is a CSS grid of buttons. None of those structures is evidence that ordered records have already been implemented.

## Policy for result data

When the content represents records with comparable columns, its relationships need to survive reading beyond the visual arrangement. CSS alone can align text while leaving those relationships absent from the document structure. Ranked or bracket data is a table element with a caption and th scope="col" header cells. The caption identifies the collection being read, while the column headers connect each record's values to their meaning.

This is a content-specific policy. It does not make the game board a data table because it has rows and columns, and it does not require converting every compact summary to tabular markup. The distinction begins with what the content means: interactive card coordinates, a property's value and a record in an ordered result collection are different things.

No such result feature is present in `Game.tsx`. The policy applies when result data is introduced. Native controls guide discusses the broader preference for native semantics without adding another result format.

## Why the statistics are a definition list

## storage-failure-policy
# Storage failure policy

This page describes how unavailable browser storage affects play and how saved-record features present that limitation.

The current game isolates storage failures from the active game. It catches errors while obtaining the browser store, reading the preference key and writing its replacement. The session can hold its selected size and best results in memory even when no durable write succeeds. There is no current preference-storage warning in the rendered game.

## Features with saved records

For a feature that presents saved records, the unavailable-storage state belongs near the data it affects. The active interaction can still use its current in-memory state even though later visits cannot rely on finding that state again. When browser storage is blocked, a feature keeps working in memory and shows "Progress won't be saved on this device." where its saved records would appear. This ties the explanation to the missing persistence rather than turning it into a failure of the whole game.

The preference adapter does not yet expose a blocked-status result. `readPreferences` returns a `Preferences` value in all cases, and `writePreferences` returns `void`. Neither return type carries an availability flag or failure reason. `Game.tsx` renders no preference-storage warning; saved-record features have separate failure feedback.

The existing status display remains driven by session state. A best achieved during a visit can appear there after a failed write because it is already in `session.preferences`. A visible best is evidence of the in-memory result; persistence across a later reload needs separate evidence. Persistence overview describes the data boundary.

## Three browser operations can fail independently

## corrupt-data-policy
# Corrupt data policy

This page explains how Neon Pairs handles unreadable or invalid stored data and how read rejection relates to a later save.

Browser storage contains strings outside the type system. A value may have been written by an older build, edited by a person, truncated by a debugging experiment or replaced by another script on the origin. The current preference reader accepts only a usable preference aggregate and otherwise returns its default. It does not try to repair individual score entries.

## Rejection at the read boundary

A failed decode produces empty application data rather than a partially interpreted value. The read path can abandon unusable content without deleting the browser string as part of that read. A stored value that fails to parse or validate is treated as empty, without any error, and stays untouched until the next save replaces it. The distinction between reading and saving matters because a save can follow immediately during application initialization.

For current preferences, “empty” is the complete fallback `{ size: DEFAULT_SIZE, bestMoves: {} }`. `DEFAULT_SIZE` is 4. The result is therefore a fresh default-size game with no known bests, rather than an empty board or a blocked screen. `readPreferences` makes that fallback before entering its `try` block and returns it from each rejection branch.

The reader has no write or removal call. However, `useSavedPreferences` runs an effect on mounting with the preferences obtained during initialization. That effect can overwrite the rejected string with valid fallback preferences after rendering. The original text remains available only until a save occurs, and the ordinary mount effect is such a save.

## Parsing is only the first filter

## target-size-policy
# Target size policy

This page records the control target policy and explains the size constraints already present in the interface styles.

Target size is about the area a person can activate, not the size of a glyph drawn inside it. A card's marker is small, but the native button enclosing the whole card is the target. The same distinction applies to a summary's disclosure marker and the much larger summary row.

## Policy and present coverage

The existing code already gives cards a minimum track size and shared controls a minimum height. Extending the interface calls for checking the actual rendered target in the phone layout, where flex wrapping and available width matter. Every new control is at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels at a 390 pixel wide viewport. This policy covers the rendered control area rather than enlarging only a decorative child or a focus ring.

The current styles are useful building blocks, but they are not proof of every dimension for an arbitrary new element. In particular, `.control` declares minimum height without a general minimum width. A new short-label action could be tall enough while still being too narrow. The policy check and the existing class definition therefore answer related but different questions.

This is a control policy, not a claim of complete accessibility conformance. The visuals specification makes the same distinction for its chosen card minimum. Names, keyboard operation, contrast, visible focus and error behavior still have their own evidence. Interface review checklist gathers those areas without turning a size measurement into a blanket result.

## Size sources in the current code

## import-safety-policy
# Import safety policy
This page explains how Neon Pairs validates untrusted exchange text before a browser session or replay result can use it.

The important boundary is between a draft and accepted game data. A text field can contain arbitrary edits, and a replay file can contain arbitrary bytes decoded as text. Neither is treated as a `GameState` just because JSON parsing succeeds. Shape checks, numeric checks and game-specific consistency checks happen before the browser commits a replacement.

## Field diagnostics and the current implementation

A field outside a format's declared shape is a validation failure, including inside a selection or replay action. The diagnostic policy makes that particular mistake identifiable to a person correcting copied data. An import with a field its format doesn't define shows "Unknown field: NAME." for the first such field and leaves the current state unchanged. This applies to the field diagnostic; it does not make an incomplete object or an unsupported version acceptable. The format's own required fields and state constraints still determine acceptance.

The implementation already rejects extra keys, but does not yet produce that field-specific notice. `hasExactKeys` returns a boolean, `decodeSnapshot` returns `null`, and the browser displays `Invalid snapshot.` for all snapshot failures. `readReplay` provides problem categories rather than the offending key name. The current adapters reject extensions without identifying the offending field as the diagnostic policy requires.

The existing code does not define a traversal order, object-path syntax or combined-error format for a field-specific diagnostic. Its boolean exact-key helper cannot report a first key. Those details cannot be inferred from a `null` result. For current behavior, examine the published notice and replay problem category rather than expecting a key name.

## Validation before replacement

`useGame.loadSnapshot(text)` calls `decodeSnapshot(text)` first. A failed result calls the notice helper and returns `false`. Only a successful result reaches `clock.reset()` and `replaceGame(current.current, game, true)`. There is no earlier step that installs the imported code or clears the existing matched positions.

## error-display-guide
# Error display guide

This page explains how failed board-code and snapshot loads are reported without replacing the current game.

The current UI has two validation outcomes that are errors: `Invalid board code.` and `Invalid snapshot.`. They describe the attempted load, not a broken game. The player can correct the draft and retry while the current deal remains available.

## The visible location

Reproduction renders a paragraph with `id="load-notice"` and class `load-notice` inside `.load-status`. That container follows the native details element. It is adjacent to the reproduction tools but outside their collapsible body.

Both Load board and Load snapshot carry `aria-describedby="load-notice"`. Their visible names remain the action labels; the description associates the nearby outcome with those actions. The field labels stay Board code and Snapshot JSON rather than being replaced with an error sentence.

Because the paragraph is outside details, it remains in document flow when the panel is closed. A person does not have to reopen the JSON field merely to see the most recent load notice or Resume. The `.load-status` flex row wraps, has a `12px` gap and a `56px` minimum height; its paragraph can grow and shrink within the available width.

The same load outcome is also published through the game's feedback path. Announcements policy describes that event handling. The local paragraph's role here is visible context beside the load tools, not a second independent validation system.

## motion-policy
# Motion policy
This page describes the motion currently used by Neon Pairs, its reduced-motion behavior, and the source and tests behind it.

The game has two authored motion effects: a card border transition and a completion pulse. Neither moves a card, changes its dimensions, or delays a game-state update. The relevant declarations live with their components in `src/game/board/card.css` and `src/game/status/status.css`. The broader visual specification is Visuals; turn timing belongs in Turn resolution.

## Card borders

The `.card` rule declares `transition: border-color 120ms ease`. On hover, `.card:hover` changes the border to `var(--text)`. A matched card instead uses `var(--green)`. The transition is limited to the border color: background, outline, size, opacity and SVG geometry have no transition in this rule.

This distinction matters when reading a recording. A reveal replaces the back with the face and changes the card background immediately. The border can still be between colors if the pointer has just entered or left the card. A screenshot taken during that interval does not show the final border value. In `tests/art.e2e.test.ts`, the comparison helper waits for the card's animations to finish before collecting computed styles for this reason.

There is no flip animation. `Card.tsx` conditionally renders either the neutral back span or the `Face` component. The face is absent while the card is closed. Adding a visual flip would therefore be more than a cosmetic adjustment to an existing transform: it would introduce an effect where the current renderer has none. The present markup and identity boundary are described in Card artwork.

Hover also has no gameplay effect. `tests/style.e2e.test.ts` records all computed properties before and after hover, checks that only border-color properties differ, and compares exported game progress. That test is useful when an apparently small visual edit adds a shadow, scale transform or other hover change. Such a difference would depart from the existing V16 behavior even if the card still looked recognizable.

## Reduced motion

## adr-058-storage-namespace
# ADR 058: Give additional stored data a distinct namespace

This record explains the naming rule for new stored data while preserving the existing preferences key.

## Context

The first storage decision used a game prefix, a data-family segment and a version suffix separated by dots. The current preferences key still demonstrates that choice: `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`. It contains a selected size and a map of per-size best moves in a versioned JSON value.

Additional stored families need a recognizable naming convention without turning a documentation change into an unnecessary migration of existing preferences. This record supersedes ADR 011. The scope is key naming; it does not add another stored family to the current game or replace snapshot export with automatic progress saving.

## Decision

The namespace distinguishes newly introduced storage from keys that a released game already reads. New stored data uses a key of the form np3:THING, where THING is a lowercase plural noun for what is stored. Keys that already exist keep their names. This lets a reader recognize the new convention while the existing preference reader continues to find its current value.

The distinction is intentionally about whether a key already exists, rather than whether its contents look old. Renaming preferences merely to make the key look consistent would require a migration, conflict handling and evidence that the saved size and records survived. No such migration is implemented in the source.

## test-policy
# Test policy

This page explains the verification layers used by Neon Pairs and the kinds of failures each layer can establish.

The repository checks rule transitions, serialized input, source conventions and complete browser journeys. These checks share documented examples but do not all run in the same environment. `npm test` runs Vitest; `npm run test:e2e` builds the current application and diagnostic entries, then uses Node's test runner with Playwright browser support.

## Focused evidence stays near behavior

The core has adjacent tests such as `game.test.ts`, `deck.test.ts`, `snapshot.test.ts` and `replay.test.ts`. Their names make the behavior under discussion easy to locate before reading the whole suite. A feature's rules.ts has a rules.test.ts beside it. Complete interaction journeys remain at the application test level, where focus, storage, browser lifecycle and delivery can be observed together.

Adjacency is useful because a transition and its evidence can be read in one pass. It does not mean every production file in the repository has a one-to-one test file. Some concerns have several focused files: completion, move limits, snapshot selection and replay ordering each get separate attention. Other helpers are exercised through a broader behavior or browser journey.

The architecture specification A10 asks for focused tests near behavior, independent literal generation vectors, transitions checked against stated rules and built HTML checked from disk as well as served. Those are different obligations because no single test environment can establish all of them.

## What Vitest includes

## competition-rounds
# Competition rounds

This page explains the stages of a shared-device bracket and the round text associated with play.

A round provides context that the card board cannot provide on its own. A participant may recognize the game immediately and still be unsure where the group has reached. This page concerns that event context; the arrangement of opponents is in competition pairing, and the dimensions of the playing board are in competition boards.

## Names during play

The round name describes a stage of the event rather than the current card selection or the number of turns taken. Name each round Quarterfinal, Semifinal or Final, and show it as "Round: NAME" while that round is played. A bracket of four has no Quarterfinal. The resulting vocabulary is small enough for a waiting participant to recognize without interpreting a bracket diagram.

For an eight-person event the names progress through Quarterfinal, Semifinal and Final. For a four-person event the names begin with Semifinal and lead to Final. These follow the naming rule.

The capital letters in the quoted pattern indicate where the round's name appears. Substituting Semifinal gives `Round: Semifinal`; substituting Final gives `Round: Final`. The pattern does not imply that the screen literally presents the placeholder. It also does not define the name of the participant who is currently using the device.

## Round, match and board are different contexts

## competition-deals
# Competition deals

This page explains deal identity in competition and the existing board-code machinery that can reproduce an arrangement.

The current engine already has a precise way to identify a starting puzzle. A board code describes its generation version, side length and seed. That identity is useful when comparing what people played, investigating an apparent discrepancy or distinguishing a fresh attempt from restored progress.

## Deal identity within an event

A match has a deal identity as well as the identities of its participants. Both players of a match play one board code, and every match in a tournament has a different board code. The identity in that sentence is the complete board code, rather than only the final numeric part or a screenshot of the visible board.

For example, a match associated with `np1-4-73` refers to the arrangement generated by that full string. A later match using `np1-4-74` has a different code. `np1-6-73` is also a different code from the first example: its side length differs even though its seed number is the same. These examples illustrate code identity without introducing a new competition-specific code format.

The distinction between board identity and progress is just as important. A hidden starting board, a board with several pairs exposed and a completed board can all have the same `boardCode`. They are different game states on the same deal. A screen showing more exposed faces does not, by itself, show that a different board was loaded.

## The format already implemented

The arithmetic never floors the delta. For observations at 0, 0.3, 0.8, 1.1, 3.7 and 10.9, adding the active steps gives the same total as one active observation at 10.9, allowing ordinary floating-point tolerance. A timer frequency change therefore does not inherently change elapsed accounting.

This framing avoided a feature checklist in which every popular addition looked like a missing requirement. Pointer timing adds a separate issue. Focusing a partly visible card on press must not move the target away before release. Each maps to an existing implementation boundary rather than a new setting.

### retention-policy.md
A list can grow as a feature saves additional records, even when every individual record is small. Its retention boundary applies during saving, rather than acting as an expiration clock while the player is idle. A stored list keeps its newest 10 records and drops older ones when a new record is saved. This bounds the retained collection while leaving the active interaction independent of an ever-growing history.
This rule concerns a saved list. It does not turn the existing `bestMoves` object into a history or add a timestamp to it. Record types, sort fields and tie-breaking conventions are separate from the amount retained. The preference store implements the best-score aggregate rather than a feature list.
For list work, the save event named by the retention rule should be understood in the feature's own operation. The existing preference effect has no generic event log or timer that scans all browser keys. There is no central list manager in this source tree.
For a feature-list review, concrete before-and-after examples can expose the retention boundary without adding fields to the product format. Records can be identified by the already defined domain representation in that feature's tests. The useful observation is which accepted records are present after a save, compared with the preceding accepted collection. Examples can use the feature's existing record fields.
It is also useful to keep failed writes separate from successful retention checks. A denied store can leave the feature's in-memory state ahead of the browser value. Inspecting the old browser string then proves only that the write failed, not that the retention calculation chose the wrong records. Storage testing guide describes the store doubles that make this separation observable.

### retired-idea-hints.md
One sketch would point toward a face that had previously been revealed. This sounded closest to ordinary remembering: the system would not disclose anything the player had never had an opportunity to see.

### retired-idea-online-play.md
The team did not choose a message protocol, room format, or hosting provider. Those would have been new implementation commitments for a feature the project had not approved. Retirement left the current app's simpler service boundary intact.

### retired-idea-themes.md
They were not actually the same scale of change. A page-background variation can leave face identity intact. Replacing the face catalogue with pictures changes what the player must recognize. Altering marker positions or removing outline fills can collapse distinctions between pairs. The review separated those consequences before trying to estimate implementation effort.

### retired-idea-timed-mode.md
An especially tempting shortcut was to retain the same best map and ignore the mode. That would make a careful untimed attempt and an urgent countdown attempt comparable only by moves, even though the new feature's purpose was speed pressure. Creating another record category would be a legitimate design task, but it would expand preference validation and the result interface.

### scoring-and-moves.md
`advanceGame` never changes moves. `activateCard` does not add elapsed duration. A logical replay can match several pairs at the same timestamp, while a visible player can spend a long time with one card revealed and still have zero moves.

### screen-reader-notes.md
The deck still exists in game state because the game must resolve matches. The DOM boundary is the important distinction for the interface: a hidden card control exposes its position and closed state, not its underlying identity. Card artwork and Pair identity explain the visual and game sides.

### selection-state.md
This shape lets `activateCard`, `faceUpCards`, and the snapshot reader branch on one field. In the activation function, the default branch calls `unreachable` with a `never` parameter. Exhaustiveness is tied to the union rather than to an informal assumption that there are only three strings.
Parsed JSON needs runtime checks. `readSelection` in `snapshot-selection.ts` checks each alternative's exact fields. A one-card index must be a nonnegative safe integer in range and absent from matched. Mismatch requires two such distinct indices with different face values and an integer remainder from 1 through 800. Closed has only its discriminant.

### snapshot-format.md
`one` means that a first eligible card has been revealed. The index must be inside the generated deck and absent from `matched`. This first reveal does not cost a move. In particular, `started: true`, `moves: 0`, no matches and a `one` selection is the normal state immediately after starting play.
Every matched index is a nonnegative safe integer smaller than the deck length. It must appear only once. The decoder counts generated face identities at those positions and requires every represented face to occur twice. An empty array is valid; an even number of positions is necessary but insufficient.
When `started` is false, all progress must be initial: zero moves, zero elapsed time, no matched positions and a closed selection. This prevents an object from combining hidden elapsed progress with an unstarted clock. It also ensures that importing an unstarted deal has a coherent state to resume.

### snapshot-selection-notes.md
At the end, every count in the map must be exactly two. Since a generated deck contains each face exactly twice, this is equivalent to asking for complete face pairs. It does not require pair members to be adjacent in the supplied array. It also does not infer pairs from the position numbers themselves.
The `one` variant has exactly `kind` and `index`. That index must pass availability. The returned object contains only the known fields, preserving the numeric position.
The exact key set is `kind`, `first`, `second`, `remainingMs`. Both positions need to be available, and they must be distinct. The generated faces then need to differ. Finally, remaining time needs to be an integer in `1..MISMATCH_MS`, where `MISMATCH_MS` is `800` from `game.ts`.

### storage-failure-policy.md
For a feature that presents saved records, the unavailable-storage state belongs near the data it affects. The active interaction can still use its current in-memory state even though later visits cannot rely on finding that state again. When browser storage is blocked, a feature keeps working in memory and shows "Progress won't be saved on this device." where its saved records would appear. This ties the explanation to the missing persistence rather than turning it into a failure of the whole game.

### storage-quota-notes.md
These figures do not include a feature's collection of records. Nor do the snapshot and replay input byte limits describe the space occupied by preferences. Those formats are separately bounded interchange text; the browser preference writer does not save either one. Persistence envelope separates the representations.

### storage-testing-guide.md
There is no useful assertion that the new board code must differ after every independent page load. Startup creates a fresh deal rather than restoring the old one, but a storage test can establish the intended state through cleared progress and retained preferences without depending on a random coincidence being impossible. New Game's seed handling is a separate behavior.

### tables-policy.md
The policy does not specify caption text. The source has no existing results title. A feature's actual subject supplies the wording. Describing that subject is different from attaching a technical explanation of table markup to product copy.

### target-size-policy.md
The existing code already gives cards a minimum track size and shared controls a minimum height. Extending the interface calls for checking the actual rendered target in the phone layout, where flex wrapping and available width matter. Every new control is at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels at a 390 pixel wide viewport. This policy covers the rendered control area rather than enlarging only a decorative child or a focus ring.

### technology.md
The browser command must fail if its build fails. It must never fall back to an earlier `dist`. Stop development servers and watchers you start before finishing the work.

### test-policy.md
The core has adjacent tests such as `game.test.ts`, `deck.test.ts`, `snapshot.test.ts` and `replay.test.ts`. Their names make the behavior under discussion easy to locate before reading the whole suite. A feature's rules.ts has a rules.test.ts beside it. Complete interaction journeys remain at the application test level, where focus, storage, browser lifecycle and delivery can be observed together.
Snapshot tests check outer keys, numeric bounds, matched-position consistency and each selection form. `snapshot-selection.test.ts` focuses on nested selection invariants. A selected index must name an available position, a mismatch must involve different faces and complete matched pairs must be represented together. The decoder reconstructs its deck from the code before checking these relationships.

### text-entry-policy.md
That distinction leaves room to implement an editing experience without confusing it with persistence. A reviewer can inspect where a completed entry crosses from local draft state into the feature's model and where the model is rendered. If display uses an old raw draft while storage uses the processed value, the two surfaces no longer have the relationship described above.

### time-policy.md
`use-session-clock.ts` owns browser observation and scheduling. Its neighbor `browser-clock.ts` accepts observations as arguments and computes a numerical step. Game code reads time only through the session clock. Only files in src/game/session/ may call performance.now, and no game code may use Date. Rule functions therefore receive elapsed amounts directly and can be exercised without a wall clock.

### unit-test-guide.md
An independent algorithm and a literal example serve different purposes. The literal catches a shared misunderstanding of the algorithm; the wider oracle comparisons catch errors that the small example does not reach. The rejection-sampling tests add stored vectors for a draw above the accepted range and a draw exactly at the limit. Ordinary seeds may never exercise either branch during a short run.

### visuals.md
- V12 - Draw each face in an SVG with `viewBox="0 0 100 100"`. Center the main shape within `x=25..75` and `y=25..75`. Draw the marker above the shape as a circle with radius 5, centered 40 units from `(50, 50)` in its marker direction. Give the marker a 3-unit stroke in the Face background color, so it stays separate from the shape. Normalize diagonal directions, giving offsets of about 28.284 units on each axis. Use a 5-unit stroke for an outlined shape. At 44px, all 128 identities must be distinguishable in a grayscale face sheet, including solid and outlined squares with diagonal markers.

### voice-guide.md
“Perfect” in the eyebrow is an atmospheric phrase about pairs. It is not a score classification. The implementation has moves, matched pairs, elapsed time and a local best move count, rather than grades such as excellent, average or poor. A release note or help paragraph that describes a “perfect rating” would create a feature the game does not have.

### win-conditions.md
Every card position must belong to a found pair. Moves and elapsed time can be large, small, or capped without changing that result. There is no losing state caused by either counter.

# ADR 041: Allow short names as typed

This historical record explains the retired one-to-thirty-two-character name limit and literal storage choice.

Status: Superseded by Name length policy

## Original context

The early name-entry discussion favored a small amount of validation. Names were expected to be short labels, not account identities, and the team wanted to avoid transforming a person's text unexpectedly. The initial rule allowed names with 1 to 32 characters and stored them exactly as typed.

That choice belonged to an earlier interface design discussion. The game has no player-name entry field in its current control tree. Its text fields are a board code and snapshot JSON, with format-specific limits.

## Decision as originally made

The lower limit excluded an empty label. The upper limit was intended to keep an entry reasonably compact on a phone while allowing more than a very short nickname. Saving the original text was meant to preserve capitalization, spacing choices and the visible spelling a person had entered.

The team treated name validation as a presentation concern rather than an identity-verification system. No account lookup or remote uniqueness check was involved. That matched the broader local-game approach: a label helped readers recognize an entry, but did not establish a trusted person behind a result.

## Reasoning

Transforming text can surprise people when the displayed result differs from the field they submitted. Literal storage looked easy to explain and easy to debug: the saved value would match the original draft. A modest length range appeared sufficient for a prototype with only a few entries.

docs/purity-guide.md:29:What matters for shared game state is that transitions do not mutate the state given to them. A new match creates a new matched array; a new selection creates a new selection object. An ignored activation returns the old state. These reference relationships are meaningful to the session commit function and board memoization.
docs/purity-guide.md:51:The snapshot decoder checks the code, bounds, matched positions and selection against a newly reconstructed deck. It checks a minimum move count and whether an unstarted state contains impossible progress. A valid result is a new `GameState`; an invalid result is null. A failed decode does not partially modify the current browser game.
docs/purity-guide.md:85:A less obvious problem is mutating an input array while returning a new outer object. That can preserve or corrupt references in ways memoized consumers do not expect. The existing transitions instead create changed collections where their meanings change and keep stable collections where they do not.
docs/randomness-policy.md:5:A new board needs an unpredictable seed. A board code, restart, imported snapshot and replay need the opposite property: a particular code always reconstructs the same deck. The implementation keeps those two tasks separate rather than letting a shuffle consult ambient state. Deck generation covers the deal algorithm as a format; this page concentrates on its source ownership and integration.
docs/randomness-policy.md:9:`src/game/session/fresh-board.ts` exports `freshBoardCode(size, previousSeed?)`. It obtains a seed and returns the normal board-code representation through `boardCode` from `deck.ts`. Only src/game/session/fresh-board.ts may call a random source. Everything else that needs randomness imports it from there. The session controller uses that exported operation when initializing a session or asking for a new game.
docs/randomness-policy.md:25:When `previousSeed` is supplied, a candidate equal to it is discarded. `use-game.ts` passes the current game's seed when creating a new game, including when a different grid size is selected. This means the next seed differs from the immediately preceding seed even across a size change.
docs/randomness-policy.md:33:Once the seed is selected, `boardCode(size, seed)` validates the representation. Its format is `np1-SIZE-SEED`, with the supported sizes supplied by `GRID_SIZES`. The parser accepts exactly the seven sizes 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14 and 16. It also checks that the seed is a safe integer within the allowed maximum.
docs/randomness-policy.md:37:The code-producing function can throw for an invalid size or seed. The session's `newGame` action checks the requested size with `isValidSize` before requesting a fresh code. Its normal UI callers use the native select populated from `GRID_SIZES`. These checks protect the application path without adding a second size list to the form.
docs/randomness-policy.md:76:This table is useful when a bug report says that “a new board changed.” A new game is expected to change the seed. A restart or imported code is expected to repeat the existing deal. A size selection is a fresh deal rather than a geometric rearrangement of the old cards.
docs/randomness-policy.md:78:`newGame` also resets the clock and replaces the session game. Seed choice alone does not clear progress or focus; session replacement and the generation key supply those lifetimes. Session module covers that process.

docs/format-versioning-guide.md:59:For an old artifact, ask whether the new reader accepts it and whether it represents the same position or actions. For a new artifact, ask whether the old reader accepts it at all. Exact-key formats often give different answers in those two directions. Recording the direction avoids a vague claim that a change is simply “backward compatible”.

 ## Where the product stands
 
-The game implements solo play. There is no competition entry form, bracket view, participant model or tournament controller in `src/game/Game.tsx`. That component composes the ordinary controls, status, board and reproduction panel around `useGame()`. Competition is a product extension that has not yet shipped.
+The game implements solo play and Tournament mode for four or eight people. `src/game/Game.tsx` composes the two screens around separate solo and tournament controllers. The entry form, bracket, handoffs, saved history and JSON exchange live in `src/game/tournament`. Tournament mode documents the complete implemented flow and interchange format.
 
 This distinction matters during review. A prototype can show a convincing bracket around the existing board while still delegating all game actions to the ordinary session. That demonstrates a possible composition, but it says little about whether participant progress, handoffs and completion belong to the same coherent experience. The detailed pages identify the relevant behavior and the places where the current source offers support or creates a complication.

This is the most consequential boundary for an extension: reusing a visual component is easy to notice, while inheriting a session side effect can remain hidden until much later.
